title: Cap. XII: Which covenant? Mosaic, Abraham, nature — no antecedent immediate before v.19
pass_a_gloss: As for the covenant, which kind does he mean? Of grace? Legal? I do not think so. Of nature? I would have him explain to me of what sort that is understood. For I see a double law was laid on Adam: one through signs naturally signifying, the other through signs signifying by institution; the former implanted in nature, the latter revealed by the word. Under the former Adam was, as man and inhabitant of the world; under the latter, as inhabitant of paradise. Which of the two was that covenant? Not the latter, as I think. For it was framed in these words: Of every tree of the garden you shall freely eat. But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat of it: for in whatever day you eat of it you shall surely die. Which law does not wear the nature of a covenant on its face, and was then laid on Adam when, for want of a wife (who was to be created supernaturally), he could not be a father. You will say that law was laid on the whole human race. Entirely it was laid on the whole human race that then existed: but not on that which neither was, nor was ever an inhabitant of paradise. Yet grant it was laid on the whole human race: ought its first actual violation, proceeding from one man, be imputed to all that man's posterity by whom it was not violated? Was not the Mosaic law laid on the whole people of Israel? And yet its first violation is not imputed to all the posterity of those to whom it was first given. Was not a covenant struck by God with Abraham? And did Abraham receive it for himself and his seed? Is therefore one or more of Abraham's actions imputed to all his posterity? Is there anything in that law from which such an imputation can be drawn? Therefore that law is not such a covenant as imports such an imputation. But neither is the law or covenant commonly called nature a covenant of this kind. Under it indeed all men are born: but in it nothing can be found from which an antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin can be gathered. For its threatenings no more belong to all men than its commands: nor are Adam's posterity any less bound each for himself to keep it than Adam once was. But perhaps I linger longer than is fair in refuting bare assertions and, as they say, petitions of principle.
pass_b_english: As for the covenant — which kind does he mean? Of grace? Legal? I think not. Of nature? Let him tell me what that is supposed to be. I see a double law laid on Adam: one through signs that signify by nature, one through signs that signify by institution — the first planted in nature, the second revealed by the word. Under the first Adam stood as man and world-dweller; under the second, as paradise-dweller. Which was 'that covenant'? Not the second, I think. It was framed in these words: Of every tree of the garden you may freely eat; but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day you eat of it you shall surely die. That law does not wear a covenant's face, and it was laid on Adam when, for want of a wife still to be created supernaturally, he could not be a father. You will say it was laid on the whole human race. It was laid on the whole race that then existed — not on a race that did not yet exist and never dwelt in paradise. Grant it was laid on the whole race: must its first actual breach by one man be imputed to all his posterity who did not break it? Was not the Mosaic law laid on all Israel? Yet its first breach is not imputed to all the posterity of those who first received it. Was not a covenant struck with Abraham for himself and his seed? Are one or more of Abraham's acts therefore imputed to all his posterity? Is there anything in that law from which such an imputation can be drawn? So that law is not a covenant that imports such an imputation. Nor is the law or covenant commonly called nature such a covenant. All men are born under it; but nothing in it yields an antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin. Its threats belong to all men no more than its commands; and Adam's posterity are each as bound to keep it for themselves as Adam once was. But perhaps I linger too long refuting bare assertions and, as they say, beggings of the question.
source_text: Ad foedus quod spectat, qualenam intelligit? Gratiae? Legale? Non arbitror. Naturae? Id quale intelligitur velim mihi exponi. Video enim duplicem latam fuisse Adamo legem: Unam per signa naturaliter significantia, Alteram per signa ex instituto significantia; illam naturae insitam, hanc verbo revelatam. Sub illa fuit Adamus, quatenus homo ac mundi incola; sub hac vero, quatenus incola paradisi. Utra foedus illud fuit? Non ista, ut opinor. His enim verbis concepta fuit, De omni arbore horti comedendo comedes. De arbore vero scientiae boni & mali non comedes ex ea: Nam quocunque die comederis ex ea moriendo morieris. Quae lex nec foederis prae se fert naturam, & tunc lata est Adamo, cum defectu uxoris (quae supernaturaliter creanda erat) pater esse non posset. Dices illam legem toti generi humano latam fuisse. Omnino lata fuit toti generi humano quod tunc extabat: at non ei, quod neque erat, neque paradisi unquam incola fuit. Fuerit tamen lata toti generi humano, num illius prima violatio actualis profecta ab uno homine, omnibus illius hominis posteris, a quibus violata non est, imputari debuit? Nonne lex Mosaica toti populo Israelitico lata fuit? Et tamen prima illius legis violatio non est omnibus posteris eorum, quibus primum lata est, imputata. Nonne foedus divinitus cum Abrahamo percussum fuit? Idque pro se & semine suo Abrahamus accepit? Numergo Abrahami actio vel una, vel plures, omnibus eius posteris imputatur? Estne quicquam in illa lege, unde eiusmodi imputatio elici possit? Non est ergo lex illa tale foedus, quod talem imputationem importet. Sed neque etiam huiusmodi foedus est lex seu foedus quod vulgo natura appellatur. Sub ea quidem nascuntur omnes homines: Sed in ea nihil potest deprehendi, unde primi Adae peccati actualis antecedens seu immediata imputatio colligi possit. Non magis enim pertinent ad omnes homines eius comminationes quam mandata: Nec minus tenentur posteri Adami pro se quisque eam observare, quam tenebatur olim Adamus. Sed fortasse diutius, quam par est, in nudis assertionibus, ac, ut loquuntur, principii petitionibus refellendis immoror.
